**Distal plantarflexor (GAS).** The gastrocnemius burst is confined to 25–38% of the gait cycle (13% duration) with a peak normalized amplitude of 0.39. This represents the single largest departure from normative data in the dataset (13.3 SD). The burst is short in duration and terminates at 38% of the cycle, i.e., before the expected terminal-stance/pre-swing period of peak plantarflexor demand. Taken together, the timing is best described as an abbreviated, mid-stance-restricted plantarflexor burst rather than the normative mid-to-terminal-stance pattern. The very large SD value indicates the profile falls well outside the normative envelope; whether this reflects amplitude, timing, or waveform shape cannot be separated from the summary statistics provided.

**Knee extensors (VL, RF).** Vastus lateralis activates at 21% and offsets at 40% (19% duration; 5.3 SD). Normatively, VL activity is concentrated in terminal swing through loading response/early mid-stance; the observed onset at 21% therefore represents a **delayed onset** relative to expected, with activity persisting into mid/late stance (**prolonged activation** relative to the normative burst window). Rectus femoris is active from 19% to 45% (26% duration; 3.3 SD). Normative RF activity is characteristically brief and biphasic (loading response and pre-swing/initial swing); a single continuous 26%-of-cycle burst spanning mid-stance constitutes **prolonged activation** with loss of the expected burst separation.

**Knee flexors / hip extensors (BF, ST).** Biceps femoris is active from 1% to 43% — a continuous burst spanning 42% of the gait cycle (3.4 SD). Onset near initial contact is timing-appropriate, but persistence to 43% indicates **markedly prolonged activation** through mid-stance, beyond the normative terminal-swing-to-loading-response window. Semitendinosus, by contrast, shows a short burst (1–8%, 7% duration) with the highest peak amplitude of any muscle sampled (0.50) and a substantial normative deviation (7.0 SD). The medial and lateral hamstrings therefore show **dissociated offset timing** (8% vs. 43%), which is not the normative pattern of broadly synchronous hamstring activity.

**Tibialis anterior.** No onset or offset could be detected, and peak normalized amplitude is the lowest recorded (0.24), with a 4.6 SD normative deviation. This is consistent with EMG activity that did not exceed the detection threshold used by the processing algorithm. Two explanations cannot be distinguished from these data alone: (a) genuinely absent or severely attenuated dorsiflexor recruitment, or (b) a technical/threshold issue (electrode placement, signal quality, or a detection threshold set relative to a low overall signal). **This finding should be treated as indeterminate pending signal-quality review.**

**Erector spinae.** A single detected burst from 4% to 10% (6% duration), amplitude 0.35, 2.5 SD from normative — the smallest normative deviation in the dataset. Normative ERS activity is typically biphasic around both double-support periods; only one burst was detected here, but with a single reported onset/offset pair it cannot be determined whether a second burst was absent or simply not resolved by the detection method.

**Co-contraction.** The RF vs. BF index of 0.81 is high and indicates substantial **sagittal-plane thigh co-contraction** (knee extensor against knee flexor/hip extensor) during the overlapping 19–43% window — a finding that is internally consistent with the prolonged, simultaneous RF and BF bursts described above. The TA vs. GAS index of 0.50 is nominally moderate, but because no TA burst was detected, **this value should be interpreted with caution**; a CCI computed against a sub-threshold or noise-dominated TA signal may not reflect true agonist–antagonist co-activation.

**Onset timing.** Five of the seven recorded muscles (RF, VL, BF, ST, TA) show onset at 0% of the gait cycle, indicating activity already present at initial contact rather than a discrete post-contact onset. With the data provided as a single onset/offset pair per muscle, it is not possible to determine whether these represent normally timed loading-response bursts that began during terminal swing, or continuous/tonic activity spanning the cycle boundary. GAS onset at 4% is early relative to the expected onset in loading response to mid-stance. ERS onset at 12% with offset at 34% is confined to a single mid-stance window; the second, contralateral-loading burst typically seen in erector spinae is not represented in these data, and its absence cannot be distinguished from a limitation of the single-burst detection output.

**Offset timing and duration.** Prolonged activation is the dominant pattern in the quadriceps and hamstring channels. RF (0–52%) and VL (0–49%) remain active through essentially the whole of stance, substantially exceeding the normative expectation of a brief loading-response burst; this is consistent with the very large normative deviations recorded for both (RF 7.3 SD, VL 6.2 SD). ST activity extends to 64% of the cycle, i.e. well past terminal stance and into early swing — the longest duration recorded and the largest normative deviation in the dataset (8.0 SD). GAS activity (4–49%) terminates at a physiologically plausible point for push-off, but its early onset yields a prolonged overall stance-phase duration and a moderate-to-large deviation (3.3 SD).

TA is active 0–20% and then no further activity is reported for the remainder of the cycle, including swing; deviation is likewise modest (1.8 SD). Whether the absence of a reported swing-phase TA burst reflects a true absence of pre-swing/swing dorsiflexor activity or a detection/reporting limitation cannot be determined from these data.

**Amplitude.** Peak normalized amplitudes cluster narrowly between 0.60 and 0.74 across all seven muscles, with no channel standing out as markedly high or low relative to the others. The large SD deviations reported appear to be driven principally by timing/duration rather than by amplitude differences among channels.

This is internally consistent with the prolonged stance-phase RF/VL activation and prolonged ST activation described above, and represents a pattern of antagonist co-contraction rather than reciprocal alternation. TA vs. GAS CCI of 0.44 indicates moderate co-contraction across the ankle; this figure should be interpreted cautiously given the restricted TA activation window (0–20%) captured in these data.
